decisions.reason: Under Step 2, nonexclusive conceptual retests of specific attributed empirical findings qualify as replications, and a paper need not retest every manipulation in an original article. Although Section II.F notes the experience tests are not directly tied to one specific study and revisit a broader stylized fact, it immediately names Hussam, Porter, and Smith (2008) under 'Replication Tests of the Experience Effect' as one of two explicit empirical comparators for testing whether trading experience reduces RD, RDMAX, and RAD between the first and second market repetitions. Inspecting the complete published Hussam et al. (2008, AER 98(3):924-937; hussam.txt) confirms that alongside their novel liquidity/dividend-variance 'rekindling' manipulation (Result 1 second sentence & Result 5, pp. 932, 936, not manipulated here), Hussam et al. explicitly test stationary baseline/replication SSW sessions across experience levels and report Result 1 (first sentence, p. 932: 'Experience reduces the amplitude of a bubble significantly') and Result 2 (p. 934: 'Experience significantly reduces the duration of a bubble'). Even though Hussam et al. p. 930 note their baseline sessions replicate SSW (1988), Huber et al. explicitly cite and compare their two-repetition test against Hussam, Porter, and Smith's (2008) published baseline experience-attenuation finding.

decisions.reason: Evaluating the outcome strictly for the retested stationary experience-attenuation finding of Hussam, Porter, and Smith (2008) (Result 1 first part and Result 2, AER 98(3):932-934, showing that experience significantly reduces bubble amplitude and duration across stationary repetitions, whereas Hussam et al.'s rekindling treatment under environment shocks is outside the scope of Huber et al.'s constant-parameter design), Huber et al. (2024) test whether RD, RDMAX, and RAD decrease significantly from the first to the second market repetition across n = 166 paired markets. All three preregistered paired t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank robustness tests are highly significant in the same direction (RD: t(165) = 8.236, p < 0.001; RDMAX: t(165) = 8.566, p < 0.001; RAD: t(165) = 7.134, p < 0.001), which the authors explicitly summarize as 'implying a replication rate of 100% for the experience hypothesis according to the statistical significance indicator' and in Section III (p. 38) as 'our replications corroborated the stylized fact that experience curbs the extent of bubbles'. Although one-sample tests show overpricing is not completely eliminated in repetition 2 (t(165) = 8.316, p < 0.001), the retested attenuation claim is unambiguously successful.
